title: When the opening habits fail: reasons and conditions
outcomes: States the condition under which each opening habit works: nothing of his own is loose and no threat is pending
Predicts when castling or a developing move is unsound because of the opponent's last move
Prefers a tactic or a defensive move to a habit when a concrete reason overrides it

steps.text: In 'Your first moves' you met three habits: a pawn in the centre, knights toward the centre, castling. Each has a reason, and the reason has conditions. When the reason is missing, the habit fails. In this lesson you test the habits. Predict first, then check.

A habit gives way to a threat. Before you use one, ask what your opponent's last move attacks. If a piece of yours is loose (attacked and not defended), or a mate is threatened, deal with that first. Then ask whether the habit's reason still holds in this position.

steps.title: Castle now?
steps.prompt: The same habit in two positions. Predict whether castling is sound in each, then check.

steps.caption: What the habit cost in the second position.

line.say: Black follows the habit and castles.
Black recaptures: a knight has gone for a pawn.
White attacks the queen and keeps developing.

steps.prompt: Think of a game where you developed quickly or castled early and still got into trouble. What had your opponent's last move done that you did not check?
